```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(cache = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE)
```

In this data challege we study how concentrated the S&P 500 is among its constituent companies. 

1. The S&P 500 (Standard & Poor's 500) is a stock market index that tracks the performance of 500 of the largest publicly traded companies in the United States.
2. It covers roughly 80% of the total value of the U.S. stock market.
3. It is a market-capitalization-weighted index. Larger companies have a much bigger impact on its value than smaller components


We will use:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyquant)
library(ineq)
```

The three packages have different roles:

```text
tidyquant    retrieve the S&P 500 constituents and weights
tidyverse    manipulate and visualize the data
ineq         calculate the Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient
```

Our main questions are:

1. How unequal are the company weights in the S&P 500?
2. How much of the index is represented by its largest companies?
3. What does the Lorenz curve tell us about concentration?
4. What is the Gini coefficient of the S&P 500 weights?


```{r}
sp500 = tq_index("SP500")
```
## 1. How unequal are the weights?

```{r}
sp500 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weight)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of S&P 500 weights is assimetric",  x = "Weight", y = "Companies")
```

The mean is much larger than the median: a few companies have very large weights, while most companies have very small ones.
```{r}
summary(sp500$weight)
```


## 2. How much do the largest companies represent?

We can see that the top 10 company represent 37% of the total weight.
Top 5 shares the 27.5%
```{r}
#let's arrange the data by weight in desc order
sp500 = sp500 |>
  arrange(-weight) |>
  select(company, weight)

#let's see how much of the index the top n companies share
sum(head(sp500$weight, 10)) / sum(sp500$weight)

sum(head(sp500$weight, 5)) / sum(sp500$weight)
```

## 3. Lorenz curve

The dashed line represents perfect equality. The curve lies far below it, so the index is highly concentrated.
```{r}
lc <- Lc(sp500$weight)

df_lorenz = data.frame(p = lc$p, L=lc$L)

df_lorenz |>
  ggplot(aes(p, L)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Lorenz curve of S&P 500 weights",
    subtitle="index is highly concentrated",
    x = "Cumulative share of companies",
    y = "Cumulative share of weight"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


## 4. Gini coefficient

The Gini coefficient is 0.711. It confirms that the Index is strongly concentrated in its largest companies.
```{r}
Gini(sp500$weight)
```
